Coline Covington   Training analyst of the Society of Analytical Psychology and the British Psychotherapy Foundation, and former Chair of the British Psychoanalytic Council. She is a Fellow of the International Dialogue Initiative (IDI), a think tank formed by Professor Vamik Volkan, Lord Alderdice and Dr Robi Friedman to apply psychoanalytic concepts in understanding political conflict. Her book publications include Terrorism and War: Unconscious Dynamics of Political Violence (co-edited with Paul Williams, Jean Arundale and Jean Knox, Karnac, 2002), Shrinking the News: Headline Stories on the Couch (Karnac, 2014), Sabina Spielrein: Forgotten Pioneer of Psychoanalysis, 2nd edition (co-edited with Barbara Wharton, Routledge, 2015), and Everyday Evils: A Psychoanalytic View of Evil and Morality (Routledge, 2016). She is in private practice in London.
DEFENCES, DISSOCIATION, FATHER, IDENTIFICATION, PSYCHIC REALITY

How do you live with the knowledge that your father ordered the death of thousands of innocent people? Children of parents who have committed or been involved in atrocities have to live with the guilt of their parents' deeds, even when guilt is acknowledged by the parents. Because of their family history, these children often become ‘lightning conductors’ for social guilt, tainted with the mark of evil. Drawing on clinical material and interviews with children of Nazi SS officers, this paper examines the personal psychological repercussions and conflicts that children of perpetrators face in their lives. These conflicts live on not only within the children who have inherited their parents' crimes but within the larger society in the form of memory, denial and guilt. The psychological dilemma for children of perpetrators provides a prism through which we can better understand the impact of past atrocities on the collective.

Tributes to Bob on His 80TH Birthday

From Nick Manning

I worked actively with Bob for about 10 years between the mid-1970s and mid-1980s, and we have kept in touch regularly ever since. I first met Bob around 1973 when I joined Henderson Hospital as a young research sociologist, at one of the first meetings of the newly formed Association of Therapeutic Communities (ATC). He was editing the ‘in house’ cyclostyled ATC newsletter, and although I can't remember in detail, we must have begun to talk about how we could develop the TC field further. At the time I had written a sociology thesis on TCs, discussing two aspects - the TC as a scientific innovation on the one hand, and on the other hand, TCs as a social movement for change in the mental health field (and beyond - as Maxwell Jones had already articulated). Indeed this was a heated focus for debate in the early days of the ATC, with radical, and often younger, staff wanting a social movement, and distrustful of the more academic and professionalizing approach from more established colleagues.

Anyhow, whichever of these was right, we reasoned that the TC field would be helpfully supported and extended by the development of a serious journal for the discussion of TC ideas. Indeed we knew from sociological work on both social movements and scientific innovation that both could benefit in this way. Bob duly formed and led a small group to explore this idea in the latter half of the 1970s, which culminated in the launch in 1980 of the International Journal of Therapeutic Communities, with Human Sciences Press (New York), and Bob as editor.

This development was quite a while in gestation, and so meanwhile he and I put up the idea to Routledge and Kegan Paul of an edited book, designed to summarize the state of the TC field in the UK, with a wide range of contributions: Therapeutic Communities, Reflections and Progress, which we edited together, came out in 1979. And on the back of that, we put up a further idea to Routledge of a TC book series. In the event, Routledge proposed that this TC series should constitute a section on Therapeutic Communities for the Routledge series International Library of Group Psychotherapy and Group Process, edited at the time by Malcolm Pines. Under our editorship from 1980, a number of significant books came out in the TC series, for example Maxwell Jones's report on his work at Dingleton Hospital, The Process of Change, and Mick Bloor's study of five TCs, One Foot in Eden. The journal, but not the book series, is still going strong.

The Greening of Psychoanalysis: André Green's New Paradigm in Contemporary Theory and Practice edited by Rosine J. Perelberg and Gregorio Kohon. Published by Karnac, London, 2017; 192 pp, £23.99 paperback

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

UK
[j.a.holmes@btinternet.com]

Jeremy Holmes  

André Green, psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, died in 2012 at the age of 84. This slim volume assembles papers from a conference hosted by the Institute of Psychoanalysis in his honour two years later. Taken together they provide a

701

fascinating glimpse into Green's ideas and influence, and to his stature and warmth as a man.

Francophone psychoanalysis is generally viewed by its anglophone counterparts with a mixture of awe and incomprehension. Every French baccalaureate candidate, we are told, is expected to be familiar with Freud; autism routinely treated with psychoanalysis; psychodynamic psychotherapy - worse still cognitive behavioural therapy - considered Coca-Cola capitalist aberrations. Meanwhile, the ‘Freud wars’ between the Lacanians and the IPA-certified psychoanalysts continue. With honourable exceptions, several of whom - Perelberg, Parsons, Kohon - contribute to this volume, French psychoanalysis remains a black box enclosed by impenetrable walls of Saussurian linguistics, post-structuralism and blithe indifference to empiricism. But here, to labour the slightly clunky pun of its title, with André's help, black turns Green, opening up a cornucopia of Winnicottian cross-fertilization and creativity.

As with many multi-author, post-conference volumes, there is some lack of coherence in the book, and it is difficult for the reader to know where best to start. The first third is taken up with Perelberg's scholarly account of the chronology and evolution of Green's ideas. This is followed by a touching short piece by Green's widow, Lisa, in which she describes the increasing distress he felt about psychoanalysis's powerlessness in the face of the violence of modern life - pre-dating Charlie Hebdo and the Paris terror attacks of the last few years. She introduces his characteristically philosophically freighted term, ‘disobjectalizing’, to describe how destructiveness is justified by dehumanizing the enemy as a thing, sub-human animal, or evil force.

Despite the book's brevity, one has to wade through a fair amount of unquestioned psychoanalytic theory (Perelberg), and enjoyable but somewhat self-indulgent excursions into contemporary Spanish sculpture (Kohon) and Greek mythology (Parsons), before getting to the core of Green's work and its relevance to everyday psychodynamic practice. For your psychotherapist-in-the-street reviewer, the core of the book is Chapter 6, a transcript of a 2011 interview by Fernando Urribanni, in which Green's voice, passion, humour and clinical skill shine through. Together with Perelberg's overview, and Urribanni's subsequent exposition (the final chapter), a number of themes emerge from the master's own account that are relevant to contemporary psychoanalytic thinking.

Silke Wiegand-Grefe   Psychologist, psychoanalyst and family therapist, Professor for clinical psychology and psychotherapy at the MSH Medical School Hamburg, Germany, and principal investigator in several funded research projects at the University Medical Centre Hamburg-Eppendorf, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry.
PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, ADOLESCENTS, CHILDREN, ANXIETY, EFFECTIVENESS, NATURALISTIC STUDY

Background The aim of the study was to look at symptom changes in naturalistic outpatient psychoanalytic child and adolescent psychotherapy for anxiety disorders in Germany.

Methods (1) The first treatment period of the psychodynamic intervention group (<25 sessions) was compared with a minimal supportive treatment (waiting list) control group, and (2) the effects of long-term psychoanalytical treatment (>25 sessions) were analysed using a longitudinal observational design. A total of 86 children and adolescents (4-21 years) were in the treatment group and 35 in the minimal supportive treatment control group. Questionnaires were administered at the beginning and end of treatment, as well as at 6- and 12-month follow-up (FU).

Results When comparing the first treatment period with the minimal supportive treatment control group, both groups improved significantly with small effect sizes and no significant group differences. Both parents and patients reported moderate symptom improvements at the end of therapy (parent: d=0.58; patient: d=0.57), which were stable at FU and increased from the patient perspective (parent: d=0.37; patient: d=0.80).

Conclusions The results suggest that anxiety symptoms significantly decreased during the treatment period and remained stable at FU. Due to the study design we could not rule out alternative explanations like regression to the mean.

[[RunningHead]]

Rozsika Parker Prize 2018

The BJP's annual Prize, established in 2013 in memory of Rozsika Parker, focuses on a critical engagement with questions of creativity. An influential art historian and clinician, Rozsika Parker represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years and was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice. The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original papers on adult, child, couple, or group psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. It is expected that authors will address the question of creativity in their submission, however broadly conceived. This may be implicit or explicit. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should also consult the BJP's submission guidelines (particularly in relation to confidentiality, where clinical material is concerned) and prepare their work with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Student path is open to students on a clinical training, who are either currently in training or who have qualified within the last 12 months; and to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. A student paper may have been submitted as part of a course requirement, if this is acceptable to the student's course, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. The Post-Qualification path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. A paper that has only been made available to an institution's membership (for example, in an internal bulletin) is eligible to be entered into the competition, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project. Manuscripts should be between 4000 and 6000 words in length including references, not including an Abstract of 200 words which should head the paper. The author's name should not appear anywhere in the body of the paper. If the paper is based on or makes use of the author's earlier published work this should be acknowledged in the form ‘(Author, date)’ within the text (i. e. the word ‘Author’ is given, plus date of publication) and there should be no entry in the References list. Manuscripts should be sent as a Word attachment to Ann Scott, Editor-in-Chief, c/o the BJP's Editorial Administrator bjpsychotherapyadmin@wiley.com

Encounters with John Bowlby: Tales of Attachment by Arturo Ezquerro. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 2017; 235 pp. £31.99 paperback

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz

[josephschwartz@btinternet.com]

Joseph Schwartz  

This is a quite unusual and very good book. Perhaps the title is badly chosen. Ezquerro isn't telling tales of attachment at all, implying something slightly mythic and fictional. Instead, it is a solid professional review of Bowlby's attachment theory, enlivened by vignettes of the author's personal relationship with Bowlby and little known historical details. Bowlby's three volume trilogy (1969, 1973, 1980) will remain the standard reference analogous to the Standard Edition of Freud's works, but Ezquerro has created a book that could serve both as a text for trainees and as an introduction for clinicians otherwise unacquainted with attachment theory. It complements and adds to the growing literature on Bowlby and his work (Fonagy, 2001; Holmes, 1993, 2015; Fonagy & Campbell, 2014; Slade, 2008).

Ezquerro was Bowlby's supervisee for six years from 1984 to 1990. As a consultant psychiatrist, psychoanalytic psychotherapist and group analyst he knows his way around the disputes and arguments that characterize our fraught discipline. His account of attachment theory covers the bases, from an account of Bowlby's childhood through to the Controversial Discussions, Bowlby's gig at the World Health Organization, and Bowlby's isolated years at the Tavistock Clinic. Ezquerro has expressed his admiration of Bowlby's contribution, doing so by summarizing attachment theory in a straightforward, matter-of-fact way, without embellishment or fan-mail.

Particularly welcome is Ezquerro's summary of Bowlby's insistence on the importance of real experience in treatment, especially in the treatment of trauma and sexual abuse. Ezquerro summarizes the conflict between Bowlby's supervision with Melanie Klein and his 10-year training analysis with Joan Riviere, and their emphasis on the inner world versus Bowlby's growing theoretical insistence on real-life experience, by quoting Bowlby's 1991 reflection:

one can only understand a person's internal world, and thus see his current situation through his own spectacles, if one can see how his internal world has come to be constructed from real-life events and situations to which he has been exposed. (p. 19)

Gertrud Mander 1927-2018

Christine Driver

Christine Driver

[chris@driver4.prestel.co.uk]

Christine Driver  

Gertrud started training as a counsellor and psychotherapist in 1976 at the Westminster Pastoral Foundation (WPF) and was one of the founding cohorts of trainees. For Gertrud, who had been a writer and journalist, this was a career change at a time in her life when she wanted to explore something new and it was clear that she had found her vocation and stepped into a journey of discovery which continued throughout her career as a therapist and supervisor. In her words, she commented that starting the training was like a ‘sunrise and the entry into a new world’. I first met her in 1978 when I started training and subsequently worked with her on both the supervision and psychotherapy trainings at WPF. Her commitment to the work and her engagement with the debates of the profession were obvious from the start.

Gertrud was inspired by her training and soon became engaged in both the work of WPF and as a supervisor in several of the WPF affiliate centres around London. This was a transformational step for Gertrud in her developing career. Learning by ‘trial and error’, and with the courage to take risks, Gertrud identified the need to develop trainings for supervisors and she approached the then Director of WPF and suggested the idea. The idea of supervision training was also in the mind of then Director, Derek Blows, and in 1985 he appointed Gertrud, together with Mary Anne Coate and Edward Martin, to start a trailblazing experiment to set up a supervision training at WPF. Gertrud became deeply involved in developing this training to ensure that it provided high standards which reflected current thinking about supervision and also met the requirements of external validating bodies. I worked with Gertrud on this training and her capacity to be both rigorous and empathic to trainees was obvious from the start. I was always impressed by her careful and detailed consideration of trainees’ progress and her gentle but firm ways of encouragement.

Gertrud was tireless in her pursuit of expanding and developing this training and together with Edward Martin, during the 1990s, took the training to Manchester, York, Birmingham, Southampton, Frome and other centres around Britain to enable practitioners from around the country to have access to training in supervision. Gertrud was involved in setting up the Group for the Advancement for Therapy Supervision which met regularly in each other's homes. However, we mostly met at Gertrud's house and her hospitality provided a place in which issues relating to supervision could be safely explored.

Stephen Crawford  

Given his title, it is perhaps no surprise that Mills takes as his epigraph Voltaire's remark that ‘If God did not exist, it would be necessary for us to invent Him’, and says that his book is about ‘the spiritual question for people who are in search of meaning and greater transcendence when they cannot believe in traditional religious principles and theological presuppositions’ (p. 2). In his opening section entitled ‘Proslogion’, after the eleventh century work by Anselm which put forward an ontological argument for the existence of God, Mills begins developing his own argument that God can only exist as an idea. Describing himself as a humanist who is in search of ‘spirituality without God’ (p. 5), he acknowledges the recent rise of writing supporting atheism, but claims a more tolerant and respectful attitude towards believers, and argues that questions about the existence of God should not be confused with questions about religion, while also expressing his interest in the psychology of belief and the different motivations that may support belief in God. While Ana-Maria Rizzuto wrote of the ‘God image’ and the ‘God representation’ (Rizzuto, 1979), Mills often writes of the ‘God posit’, a term which to my ear aims to bring the idea of God very much down to earth. Mills presents Anselm's ontological argument for the existence of God as follows: ‘God is the greatest of all possible things we can conceive … and since actuality is greater than just an object of thought or understanding … God must exist in reality’ (p. 15). He argues against this, quite reasonably in my view, saying that the fact that something may be an object of thought cannot of itself guarantee that that ‘something’ exists. He then goes on to present a set of axioms, in the form of numbered sequences of propositions, under the heading of ‘God as Thought Experiment’ (p. 32), which consider the definition of God, the existence of God and the non-existence of God, and concludes that ‘God cannot exist without mind’ (p. 38); in other words, that God is a human invention. These axioms are presented without further comment and are not referred to, as far as I could see, elsewhere in the text, and for me, seemed to stand rather outside the body of the book. The ‘Proslogion’ and the ‘Axioms’ together make up the introduction to the book.

Rozsika Parker Prize 2018

The BJP's annual Prize, established in 2013 in memory of Rozsika Parker, focuses on a critical engagement with questions of creativity. An influential art historian and clinician, Rozsika Parker represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years and was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice. The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original papers on adult, child, couple, or group psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. It is expected that authors will address the question of creativity in their submission, however broadly conceived. This may be implicit or explicit. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should also consult the BJP's submission guidelines (particularly in relation to confidentiality, where clinical material is concerned) and prepare their work with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Student path is open to students on a clinical training, who are either currently in training or who have qualified within the last 12 months; and to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. A student paper may have been submitted as part of a course requirement, if this is acceptable to the student's course, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. The Post-Qualification path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. A paper that has only been made available to an institution's membership (for example, in an internal bulletin) is eligible to be entered into the competition, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project. Manuscripts should be between 4000 and 6000 words in length including references, not including an Abstract of 200 words which should head the paper. The author's name should not appear anywhere in the body of the paper. If the paper is based on or makes use of the author's earlier published work this should be acknowledged in the form ‘(Author, date)’ within the text (i.e. the word ‘Author’ is given, plus date of publication) and there should be no entry in the References list. Manuscripts should be sent as a Word attachment to Ann Scott, Editor-in-Chief, c/o the BJP's Editorial Administrator bjpsychotherapyadmin@wiley.com

Jan Hepburn  

Thirty years after working on the collection of papers which produced what could be described as the defining overview of the Independent position in British psychoanalysis at that time (Kohon, 1986), in this book Kohon has both revisited the field and refined his thinking. He has used many of the papers which are part of the 1986 volume, and kept the four central themes: early environment, the therapeutic encounter, regression and female sexuality. However, as Kohon notes in his introduction (p. 5), this is not a new edition of an old book: it is an extension and development of how he sees the Independent tradition in today's British psychoanalytic context. As such, there are seminal papers in each section which will be familiar friends (and sometimes adversaries) to psychoanalytic readers. There are also some papers from the 1986 book which have been omitted. Kohon describes the problem of choosing from current thinkers as well as the previous papers being very similar to the problem of choosing 30 years ago, and he has tried to put together something which both elucidates the current thinking and offers the reader a satisfying experience with food for thought. He has done this partly by offering a careful and interesting analysis of the history and progression of the Independent tradition before the reader begins to tackle the papers, and includes a chapter by Perelberg in this first section. These orient the reader so that the detailed meat of the thinking is more easily digested. Another way of helping the reader's digestive processes as well as honouring some current thinkers in the field has been to begin each of the four sections with a new chapter looking specifically at the areas in the light of current knowledge.

Josh Cohen writes of earliest infancy in the light of knowledge from infant research, which was not much available when the Independent tradition was in its own early infancy.

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

bjp@ann-scott.net

Ann Scott  

It goes without saying that clinical thinking is deepened by being located within contemporary or historical debates over theory. This principle, so familiar to us, is richly illustrated in the papers in this issue of the BJP; each has its specific starting point, its own network of reference.

The issue opens with Marina Gulina and Vera Dobrolioubova's thought-provoking exploration, in our Research strand, of the lived experience of bilingual psychotherapists. Noting Freud's view of the analytic process as a process of translation, the authors scrutinize their interview data with both theoretical linguistics and the psychoanalytic approach to interpretation in mind. Participants' responses concerning ‘cultural background, behavioural nuances, vocabulary, the music of speech, meanings, feelings, symbolism, and communications’ will enable readers to reflect further on this most complex of settings.

The four papers in our regular Clinical and Theoretical Practice strand focus on different aspects of the clinical encounter. Leezah Hertzmann's vivid contribution seeks a ‘deeper understanding of the difficulties with conscious and unconscious same gender sexual desires in psychoanalytic psychotherapy’. As she says, while the paper's theoretical focus is on lesbian relationships in relation to the oedipal mother, ‘the relevance of the ideas…for other gender pairings is explored’. Next, and working within a Kleinian and post-Kleinian framework, Raman Kapur poses the evocative question: what emotional experience settles a disturbed frame of mind, a mind dominated by ‘chaos, fragmentation and feelings of “falling to pieces”?’. Kapur looks at the impact of his interpretations on the patient's state of mind, always returning to the dynamic of ‘what to say and do (or not say and do) next’. Jack Nathan, in a valuable development of earlier, co-authored work on ‘benign authority’ in work with severe borderline patients, roots his discussion in the work of Kernberg on limit-setting and of Gabbard & Westen on therapeutic actions. A specific focus on ‘maternal’ and ‘paternal’ functions and engagement, on the part of the therapist, is brought to bear on case material concerning self-harm or suicide threats. Lastly, Hanoch Yerushalmi proposes an interesting new emphasis, in supervision, on the supervisee's ‘unformulated knowledge’ of their patient, and on the supervisee's intuitive grasp of the patient's ‘unthought experiences’. This new emphasis, he suggests, in a paper whose provenance lies in the work of - among others - Bion, Bollas and Ogden, may allow the supervisor to add a new dimension to his or her work and thus be of optimal help to the supervisee.

EMOTIONAL DISTURBANCE, INTROJECT, PATHOLOGICAL ORGANIZATION, DEVELOPMENTAL DISTANCE

What emotional experience settles a disturbed state of mind? In this paper I use the work of three psychoanalytic clinicians (John Steiner, Eric Brenman and Henri Rey) to describe the negative state of mind of a patient and draw on clinical material to illustrate my efforts to settle deep emotional disturbance. Recognizing the size of the emotional task by conceptualizing the depth and breadth of the pathological organization, along with thinking carefully about the ingredients of a ‘strengthening introject’ and locating an ‘introjective site’, taking into account the developmental disparity between therapist and patient are all seen as essential countertransference processes required to facilitate movement from a bad to a good state of mind.

Juliet Newbigin  

This is a big book, in a literal and metaphorical sense. It was several years in the making, and takes the form of a compendium of 27 chapters by different authors, plus the useful Introduction and Afterword by the editors. In her Introduction, Noreen Giffney describes it as ‘structured around a series of encounters’ (p. 37), and the book is set out as an interdisciplinary discussion. It is divided into three sections: six chapters from academics, from the perspective of queer theory; 13 chapters from psychoanalytic clinicians, responding to the material in the first section; and finally, seven chapters by a range of authors, from both clinical and academic backgrounds, commenting on the issues raised by the ‘encounter’ in the preceding sections. The psychoanalytic clinicians come from a variety of backgrounds - object relations, Jungian, Kleinian and Lacanian thinking, individuals working with both adults and children. The collection comprises established and newer writers on the themes.

For the potential reader who is familiar with the term ‘queer theory’, the book's essential premise may be obvious. ‘Queer theory’ describes the work of the loosely defined range of thinkers who have emerged in the wake of poststructuralist philosophy and have taken as their starting point a critique of society's prevailing heteronormative values, energized by the moral panic caused by the AIDS crisis. Although opposed to the established forms of psychoanalytic practice, which have tended to reinforce normative assumptions about sexuality, queer writers have used psychoanalytic ideas as a tool for questioning those very assumptions. For example, Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick (1998), one of the formative writers of queer theory, says: ‘It is time for genetic narratives like psychoanalysis (and, of course, all narratives are genetic narratives) to stop representing the idiot perseveration of the assaultive and sinister question, Where do homosexuals come from’ (p. 95). Although clinicians and writers from a ‘queer’ perspective are critical of psychoanalysis, they use the same language and therefore the ‘encounter’ offered by this book is an attempt to communicate across differences. Noreen Giffney, in her introduction, points out that the book's intention is to inspire dialogue, ‘to keep a space open for different views existing alongside one another’ (p. 37).

Sometimes the Journal opens with a current clinical dilemma - most directly, perhaps, in our Clinical Commentaries, which take us straight into the here-and-now of the consulting room. Sometimes, as here, the historical and conceptual basis of our work is front and centre stage. The first three papers in this issue, within our Clinical Practice and Theory strand, address significant developments in Kleinian, Winnicottian and Lacanian thinking respectively.

The first two contributions revisit classic papers. Bob Hinshelwood investigates Hanna Segal's modification of her conceptualization of symbolic equation and symbolic representation in the light of Bion's development of the theory of container/contained. Hinshelwood scrupulously charts Segal's discussion of different types of projective identification ‘as the origin of the symbolic equation’, noting that questions of fragmentation, the role of aggression, and the representation of internal objects remain to be clarified. As he says, ‘the theory requires modifications to iron out the issues that currently flaw this powerful clinical tool’. Next, Chris Brogan considers Winnicott's work on the value of depression: ‘[b]y stating that depression has value, Winnicott challenges the view that depression is an enemy which has to be defeated… Instead he states that there is a paradox: on the one hand depression has value, and on the other it can cause suicide and intense suffering.’ Brogan carefully places Winnicott's discussion of depression alongside Klein's and Freud's, remaining inward with Winnicott's ‘startling’ idea that clinicians ‘use the patient's depression to deal with our own depression’.

Joachim Cauwe and Stijn Vanheule then address the question of transference in psychosis from a Lacanian perspective, noting the evolution in Lacan's thinking from the classical focus on the theory of foreclosure to his later discussion of experiences beyond the limits of language. ‘Transference in psychosis’, they write, ‘remains at the level of duality and appears to have an inverted form, where it is the Other that looks for something in the patient and not vice versa. This makes the handling of transference challenging since there is no triangular structure that can mediate between the patient and the Other.’ They illustrate the complexity of the therapeutic task in this most difficult of situations with a subtle account of work with a middle-aged male patient, focusing both on his melancholy, disengaged personal situation and on questions of technique.

Zelda Knight PHD

Zelda Knight

[zknight@uj.ac.za]

Zelda Knight   Experienced practising psychotherapist as well as a Professor of Psychology at the University of Johannesburg. She has been an academic for more than two decades and taught and supervised research for the same length of time in the field of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. She has published widely in international journals and books, including two recent edited books on psychoanalysis, published in New York by Nova Science. She has presented papers at numerous conferences worldwide, and given several keynote addresses at such conferences. Currently, she is Vice President of the World Council for Psychotherapy (WCP) (African Chapter) and is actively involved in promoting psychotherapy by, for example, organizing international psychotherapy conferences. She is also an ‘NRF Rated’ scientist in her country in the field of psychotherapy, a reviewer for several international journals, and has been a visiting scholar to the University of Valencia.
NAMES, INTERGENERATIONAL, FAMILY, PSYCHOANALYTIC THERAPY, UNCONSCIOUS

Names and naming practices have been the focus of social science research for several years. Our name, as part of our identity, shapes and defines our sense of self. When clients start psychotherapy they first introduce themselves by giving their names. Sometimes they speak the names of their parents and grandparents. This speaking of the collective intergenerational familial names is termed ‘speaking the names’. This article sets out to explore and describe the experience of clients in psychoanalytic therapy of ‘speaking the names’. The methodological approach is phenomenological with a focus on experience as a legitimate unit of investigation. Transcripts of sessions with clients are analysed using thematic analysis. The main exploratory findings are that ‘speaking the names’ is a significant psychological event and it can be understood as (1) ‘speaking one's place’ within the family, (2) ‘speaking the hope’ of the family, (3) ‘speaking its lived meaning’ when the meaning of their name is unknown but appears to be lived unconsciously, and (4) ‘speaking a lost connection’ when the familial names are unknown.

Monika Loewy

[m.loewy@gold.ac.uk]

Monika Loewy  

Jean Laplanche's method ‘requires the continual traversal and analysis of Freud's oeuvre … in order to re-open psychoanalysis to creative rethinking and renewal’ (p. 27), write John Fletcher and Nicholas Ray in the introduction to their collection. While this quote reflects the content of this book it also echoes its form, as it is itself an analysis of Laplanche's oeuvre that re-opens psychoanalysis to creative rethinking. This fascinating and unique book opens with an introduction that surveys Laplanche's notions of ‘exigency’, the ‘enigmatic signifier’, and the ‘theory of seduction’, which acts as a springboard for the essays on visual art, film, culture and literature that follow in the first section of the book. Although they tackle dense theoretical concepts, the essays are accessible and compelling, and bring seemingly abstract theories to material experiences and bodies of work. The central thread involves Laplanche's discussions about the ‘decentring’ of the human subject, about how we are shaped by the ‘other’ and how this translates to social and cultural realities and texts. This theme is explored in the first section through three essays by Laplanche, which provides the backdrop for the second section, which is composed of two essays about sexuality and gender; the two final sections examine metapsychology through a variety of cultural works.

Appropriately, in the first essay Laplanche addresses the theme of interpretation ‘in’ Freud and ‘of’ Freud; the manifest and latent, conscious and unconscious text. This essay spills into the following, entitled ‘Exigency and going-astray’, wherein he deals with how ‘exigency’ and ‘going astray’ are connected to the ‘Copernican revolution’. Freud's work, Laplanche explains, is associated with the Copernican decentring of the human (as Copernicus decentred the human when he demonstrated that the sun did not revolve around the earth), because the ‘unconscious decentres man in relation to himself’ (p. 24); the unconscious, in other words, makes one alien to oneself. However, he suggests that Freud proceeded to ‘recentre’ the human, and thus returns to Freud's work, not to critique it, but to find its fissures and decentre the subject once again. For him, studying Freud's work in this way may provide new pathways for thinking about the psyche.

Lesley Caldwell

Lesley Caldwell

[l.caldwell@ucl.ac.uk]

Lesley Caldwell  

505

‘Monomaniac of gambling’, from the Louvre, one of a series of five portraits by Gericault, probably painted in the early 1820s, provides the cover image of Robert Snell's new book, a scholarly account of the artistic, social, medical and philosophical discourses through which the twentieth century subject of psychotherapy emerges and is established. The painting draws the observer immediately through the artist's rendering of the eyes and his lighting of the face and head. The quality of this image is particularly noteworthy, since all the other images are black and white, and of indifferent quality. The cover design itself is worth lingering over in that its juxtaposition of text and image anticipates some of the areas the author is attempting to bring together in his study. The text of the title partially obscures this one colour image; in doing so, it directs attention to the upper part of the sitter's face and its profound, clear-eyed melancholy, while indirectly challenging the author's close attention to this image and to the group of images he discusses so sensitively throughout. Given Snell's art historical credentials, the placing of the title across the mouth and lower face may be intended to further emphasize the sitter's anonymity and the obscure histories of all five of Gericault's subjects; a feature Snell notes as part of the artist's decision to portray their normality, their ordinariness.

For me, however, before even opening Robert Snell's fascinating book, the juxtaposition of image and word and the former's apparent subordination to the latter, registers an aspect of this book's overall shape, that is, the array of subjects being investigated is so dense and so compellingly addressed that the paintings themselves can sometimes seem at risk of disappearing. This would be to do Snell an injustice, however, because a close attention to these images and their complex history is certainly there. It does perhaps signal an occasional need to search for them amidst the mass of related scholarly detail that also confronts us. In compensation for the book's lack of images, Snell advises going to his website to view the portraits and associated images in better conditions. This is sage advice since his study of the emergence of the modern individual as also the study of the emergence of the subject of psychotherapy begins from these images, Gericault's portraits. In that lies both the artist's centrality and the book's distinctiveness. Snell proposes that through the decision about how to represent his sitters, the artist visually anticipates that quintessentially modern figure, the subject of psychotherapy.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

With this issue of the Journal we are marking its founder Bob Hinshelwood's 80thbirthday in December this year, and we wanted to record this significant moment in a variety of ways. We offer an interview with him about the Journal and its history, a group of personal tributes, and a debate around his work on psychoanalytic research. In a candid interview, he says he will offer ‘rambling free associations - but what could be more appropriate?’, and the reader learns much, among other things, about the clinical and political context in which the BJP was formed. The ten tributes that follow, from national and international colleagues, provide a personal glimpse of Bob's capacity for close engagement and for the development of shared projects.

Then, in ‘Psychoanalytic research: Personal reflections’, Bob Hinshelwood argues for the importance of clinical research ‘on the couch’. He explores the question of subjectivity ‘in contrast to the bedrock of objectivity in the natural sciences’; and the question of single-case research as opposed to large-sample research, within psychoanalysis. We have three responses to the paper. Anna Ursula Dreher, warmly recognizing that Hinshelwood is ‘one of the rare bridge-builders between psychoanalytic theory traditions as well as between research traditions’, supports the analytic situation ‘as core, as context of discovery as well as context of justification’, but does not regard the hypothetico-deductive logic of experiment as a suitable paradigm for research on the couch. Stephen Briggs also acknowledges Hinshelwood's work as ‘monumental in developing clarity and focusing on re-evaluating the basis of psychoanalytic knowledge’. Writing from a social science perspective, he acknowledges the ‘powerful lure’ of physics, but argues both that psychoanalysis ‘has characteristics of, and makes contributions to, social sciences’, and that ‘changing contexts affect practice profoundly’. In my own Response I write as the current editor of the Journal, and respond to the research challenge Bob Hinshelwood has identified for the BJP. I do so by tracing the history of research publishing in the Journal; I also look at the evolution of Hinshelwood's views on research, making use of Edward Said's work on late style in drawing a contrast between the views expressed now, and views expressed in earlier years. We have invited Bob to respond to the Responses to his paper, and his Response will be published in the next issue of the Journal.

THEORY, SUBJECTIVITY, PRACTICE, REFLEXIVITY, SOCIAL SCIENCE, TECHNE, CONTEXT DEPENDENT

This response welcomes Bob Hinshelwood's plea for research in the psychoanalytic setting, and his discussion of processes for clarifying concepts and for the comparative examination of different positions. I suggest that the aims of Hinshelwood's project could be more effectively realized within a social science approach and discuss some implications for ways of conceptualizing science, theory and subjectivity. I suggest that the focus for research within the psychoanalytic setting should include how clinical practice is evolving under changing social contexts.

R.D. Hinshelwood

R.D. Hinshelwood

[bob.hinsh@gmail.com]

R.D. Hinshelwood   Fellow of the British Psychoanalytical Society and a Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists. He is Professor Emeritus at the University of Essex, and previously Consultant Psychotherapist in the NHS, and Director of the Cassel Hospital. He has published a number of books on Kleinian psychoanalysis, including A Dictionary of Kleinian Thought (1989) and Clinical Klein (1994), as well as a psychoanalytic understanding of psychiatric practice, including Suffering Insanity (2004) and (with Wilhelm Skogstad as co-editor) Observing Organisations (2000).
RESEARCH, SUBJECTIVITY, SINGLE CASE STUDIES, HYPOTHETICO-DEDUCTIVE METHODOLOGY

In this paper I reflect on and argue for the importance for our profession of the issues I address in the book I wrote on clinical research, Research on the Couch: Subjectivity, Single Case Studies and Psychoanalytic Knowledge. Psychoanalytic theories, often dismissed when first proposed, have been subjected to more serious critical attack for several decades, and thoughtful responses need to be given. This paper summarizes some of my thinking (and that of others) around two issues which constrain the parameters of psychoanalytic research and on which some believe psychoanalytic research has foundered. The first is the problem of subjectivity in contrast to the bedrock of objectivity in the natural sciences; and the second is the inappropriateness of large sample research (as used by many experimental psychologists) for the task of investigating the nature and effectiveness of psychoanalysis. Psychoanalysts have to rely instead on single cases. Brief accounts are given here of research paradigms appropriate to the investigation and validation of psychoanalytic theory and practice.

Open Letter from a Group of Jungians on the Question of Jung's Writings on and Theories about ‘Africans’

Andrew Samuels

Andrew Samuels

[andrew@andrewsamuels.net]

Andrew Samuels  

Dear Editor,

Thirty years ago, the British Journal of Psychotherapy published a paper by Dr Farhad Dalal entitled ‘Jung: A racist’ (Dalal, 1988). Regrettably, no adequate acknowledgement or apology for what Jung wrote, and Dalal critiqued, has been forthcoming from the field of analytical psychology and Jungian analysis. (To contextualize what follows, the Abstract to Dalal's paper has been placed in an Appendix to this letter.)

We write now as a group of individuals - Jungian analysts, clinicians, and academics utilizing concepts from analytical psychology - to end the silence. We felt further encouraged to write to the BJP in particular because of the Journal's strapline making clear its interest in ‘Jungian practice today’.

Via detailed scholarship, Dalal sets out what Jung wrote about persons of African and South Asian Indian heritage, as well as other populations of colour, and Indigenous peoples. Before and since the paper, Jung's views have caused considerable disquiet and often anger within the communities concerned. There has also been disquiet and anger about Jung's views in clinical, academic and cultural circles generally. Analytical psychologists and other Jungians have known about the implications of Jung's ideas for decades; there are signatories to this Letter who have campaigned for recognition of the problems. But there has been a failure to address them responsibly, seriously and in public.

We share the concern that Jung's colonial and racist ideas - sometimes explicit and sometimes implied - have led to inner harm (for example, internalized inferiority and self-abnegation) and outer harm (such as interpersonal and social consequences) for the groups, communities and individuals mentioned in the previous paragraph. Moreover, in the opinion of the signatories to this letter, these ideas have also led to aspects of de facto institutional and structural racism being present in Jungian organizations.

In this interview by email, Bob Hinshelwood responds to a set of questions about the BJP from the current Editorial Board. The questions focus on the Journal's origins and development, and on the nature of its project. What was the gap, what was he trying to do? How long did it take to get a Journal into print? What questions did he try to answer? How were the politics of the early days? What were the highlights and lowlights in ownership of the Journal? Is he pleased to see the Clinical Commentaries return? How does he feel about the Journal's relationship with psychoanalysis? How would he like to be remembered? In his responses he emphasizes the personal nature of his recollections, rather than a setting down of historical fact.

Writing as the current editor of the BJP, I respond to the research challenge Bob Hinshelwood has identified for the Journal. I explore the history of research publishing in the BJP, noting the evolution of the Journal's Aims and Scope statement, and the wide range of research methodologies and topics that have been represented. I trace the evolution of Hinshelwood's views on research, making use of Edward Said's work on late style in drawing a contrast between the views expressed in Hinshelwood's ‘Psychoanalytic research: Personal reflections’, and views expressed in earlier years.

Charlie Severo , Pricilla Laskoski , Stefania Teche , Ana Bassols , Raquel Saldanha , Rafael Wellausen , Aline André Wageck , Camila Da Costa , Diego Rebouças , Carolina Padoan , Alcina Juliana Barros , Maria Lucia Nunes and Cláudio Eizirik

Cláudio Eizirik

[ctsevero@gmail.com]

Cláudio Eizirik   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, a doctor of medical sciences: psychiatry, and a full professor of psychiatry at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul and the Psychoanalytical Society of Porto Alegre, Porto Alegre, RS, Brazil.
PSYCHOANALYTIC ENACTMENT, TRANSFERENTIAL AND COUNTERTRANSFERENTIAL RELATIONSHIPS, INTERSUBJECTIVE RELATIONS, ANALYTIC DYAD, ANALYTIC PROCESS, PSYCHOTHERAPEUTIC PROCESS, PSYCHODYNAMIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, ANALYSIS

Ongoing studies in psychoanalysis have been broad and progressive, and have dealt with a number of different phenomena. Many thus foster the identification of intersubjective aspects that characterize therapeutic relationships today, including enactments. The concept of enactment first appeared in the literature in the mid-1980s and was defined as a manifestation where, in the analytic situation, both analyst and patient unconsciously ‘play out’ psychic conflicts that must be worked out therapeutically. Resulting from unconscious forces activated mutually by the members of a therapeutic dyad, enactments are characterized by transferential and countertransferential dynamics. They are based on the mechanism of projective identification, which is interpersonal and intersubjective. In preparing the present systematic review, PUBMED, PsycINFO and LILACS databases were consulted, a process that generated a total of 59 articles. This paper gives an account of articles published on enactment, including authors, journals, year, type of study and diagnoses, as well as the gender and age bracket of patients mentioned in the literature investigated. We specifically describe how the authors of the respective articles understand and identify the concept of enactment and how they deal with this phenomenon in their clinical work.

Julian Masters  

This dense but rewarding book of essays boasts an impressive array of writers, hailing mainly from the UK and the US but also with contributors from Italy, South Africa and Switzerland. The content of the book ranges across a broad array of topics, pitching Jungian and post-Jungian theory not only against (and with) Freud but also, Lacan, Kohut, Benjamin, Bion and Klein. Contemporary findings from the fields of attachment and developmental psychology are also brought to the table.

The scene is set beautifully by R.D. Hinshelwood in a short essay about the pioneering days of psychoanalysis in which he takes the heat off the principal players and focuses attention instead on the choruses in their respective cultural habitats of Zurich and Vienna. Hinshelwood remarks; ‘each group had a history, a certain place in the world, specific aims and a characteristic culture’ (p. 20).

This was all a long time ago and, as remarks Angela Connolly in her essay (‘the iconic and aesthetic turn in depth psychology’), ‘We are now in a position to critique the theories of our illustrious predecessors’ (p. 73). This attitude is, I think, realized throughout the book by the variety of ways these writers attempt to chart the perilous waters between the Scylla and Charybdis of Freudian and Jungian traditions.

Rapprochement is of course only feasible when the ground has been prepared, where there is already a loosening of sharp and hostile tribal distinction.

Diana Birkett  

The title of this book struck me at first as something of a tautology, for what is experience if it is not lived? But, like the book itself, it contains a density of meaning that unfolds over the five chapters of Parts l and ll, and is illustrated by personal experience in Part lll.

The author aims to present the crucial difference between experience mediated by the left and right sides of the brain. In this she draws heavily on Iain McGilchrist's

161

now classic The Master and his Emissary(2009), and not the least aspect of her contribution is to make his fascinating neurological study more accessible for use by psychotherapists. ‘Briefly, the right hemisphere involves the intuitive, implicit, mostly unconscious, sensory-based experience, in the moment, which remains open, receptive, and wide ranging. It comes online in development before the left hemisphere and remains oriented to the input from the body but also to otherness in terms of the world beyond the bodily self’ (p. 5). The functions of the left, in contrast, ‘which become active from about 18 to 24 months of age, are those which link to the realm of conscious control of oneself and the environment as it relates to the world. These include fine-motor co-ordination, development of language, manipulation of objects’ (p. 6). While recommending the optimal integration of these two ‘ways of being’, she follows McGilchrist in warning against the overvaluation of left-brain functions, which are described as having a tendency to control, rationalize and dominate both the natural world and modern society (increased pressure towards bureaucratic procedures are an example of this tendency: the map can come to be taken for the terrain it represents, and measuring phenomena take the place of appreciating them).

Anderson found herself feeling increasingly alienated by the psychoanalytic leaning towards ‘parsing reality’ and ‘idealising texts and theories as if they hold deeper wisdom than does one's own experience’ (p. xix). This would be a left-brain leaning towards certainty and intellectual domination, at the expense of a more wide-ranging, intuitive approach. Paradoxically, the science of neurology would seem also to land in the left-brain camp, being based on close observation, objectivity, measurement and experiment: but it becomes an ally when it uncovers ‘the primacy of affect’, as described by Solms (1997), who ‘notes that the precursors of our cognition lie in the affective upwellings triggered by the brainstem, and so all cortical presentations of these manifestations are hallucinatory in origin as they arise from internal sources’ (p. 59). In other words, affect predates cognition, just as right-brain functions predate the left. By ‘hallucinatory’, I understand Solms to mean derived from an internal unconscious, rather than from a perception of the external world, but the lovely word ‘upwellings’ (Anderson's own) may describe it better. This is where the title of the book becomes clearer: experiences have to be lived to become conscious, and then they can be fixed in explicit memory. Implicit memory is more like that feeling on awakening from a dream, a feeling rather than a factual memory.

This paper has been five years in the making, since I have run a series of seminars about poetry and psychoanalysis at the Tavistock Clinic for non-clinical students. The title comes from a poem by John Berryman (1914-72), ‘Dream Song 29’ (1964, p. 77), and it sums up how in this seminar we have tried both to feel what we feel in an authentic way when reading a poem, and think about the links it may have with the central core of the students' study, which is psychoanalysis. Are the two disciplines in any way complementary? Can unconscious phantasy be tapped into via the medium of poetry? In this paper I hope to show that while there are profound differences between poetry and psychoanalysis there are also similarities, as the work with students has highlighted. I also include three brief clinical vignettes.

Coline Covington has written before on the subject of human destructiveness, and has accumulated a body of knowledge around some of the most extreme historical manifestations of cruelty, such as civil war, the use of torture, and genocide. She ends this book with a question: ‘Do we need a theory of evil?’, and opens it with an overview of some of the psychoanalytic theories that have attempted to answer this. Freud's term ‘the narcissism of minor differences’ (1917) describes how an unstable sense of self, provoked by certain circumstances which threaten it, leads to fending off innate aggression by turning it towards the other, one's closest neighbour, who is turned into a stranger. Winnicott (1989), writing on aggression as a crucial component of the love-impulse dispenses with the Death Instinct, and stresses that aggression is not merely a reaction to frustration, though frustration in adulthood can lead to a regression to ‘pre-ruth’, a total loss of concern for the other. This is where a more sociological dimension is needed to explain perverse group behaviour: Covington moves on to outline ‘the complex set of dynamics, fuelled by histories of fear and humiliation and impotence, which can so easily trip over into atrocity’ (p. 3).

Hannah Arendt's much quoted theory of ‘the banality of evil’ (1973) is a first attempt: she distinguishes between ‘banal evil’ and ‘radical evil’ (characterized by individual omnipotence and an intention to destroy the other). She argues that Adolf Eichmann's ‘banality’ was characterized by an absence of thought. Circumstances of extreme socio-political change, accompanied by a violent ideology, can cause a group to substitute individual conscience with a failure to think from the standpoint of someone else. Instead, normal empathy and the superego are replaced by a perverse ego-ideal projected into the leader and the group (reprising some of Freud's ideas on group psychology), and subservience to a collective fantasy. In this way evil acts are easily perpetrated by ‘nobodies’, incapable of thought or intentionality, and therefore of remorse.

This book makes a significant contribution to understanding a topic that still has not found its place within the psychoanalytic literature. Migration is a complex phenomenon and it is characterized by the interrelation of the external and the intrapsychic world. Psychoanalytic thinking is mostly preoccupied with internal processes, so the influence of the concrete, spatial environment upon the psyche has not been thought about enough. Salman Akhtar comments in an interview given at UCL (2016) that what the immigrant is longing for is not the people but the landscape, the familiar objects. According to Akhtar the human experience can be revived in the new country by associating with people alike but the objects cannot be re-found, they are permanently left behind in the home country. Dorothy Girouard  

The Metapsychology of Christopher Bollas: An Introduction is written by Sarah Nettleton, the interpretative accompanist to Bollas, the celebrated soloist. Bollas has written 13 books (the latest, Meaning and Melancholia, published in March 2018). He was awarded the Hans Loewald Award in 2006 for outstanding contributions to psychoanalysis. At the same time, neither his name nor his books have been mentioned in my or colleagues’ trainings. I first knew of his work, as I imagine many others have, via attending Sarah Nettleton's ‘Seminars on Christopher Bollas’, which she's offered around the world. Sarah Nettleton is a musician who subsequently trained as a psychoanalyst. In her first profession she worked as a piano accompanist. In a BPF ‘Audience with Authors’ in 2017 she said that the role of accompanist is often misunderstood. If the accompanist sees her role as following the soloist, she is always behind. Rather the accompanist has to be in harmony with the soloist, working in parallel. As she does with Bollas.

Sarah Nettleton, who worked with Bollas for many years as his editor, wrote this book without Bollas’ knowledge. She then sent the manuscript to him, uncertain of his reaction. In the event he was ‘bouleverse’, an untranslatable sensation, of which the closest English words are, ‘bowled over’, ‘flabbergasted’. He said she'd made connections he'd never seen. She'd given his way of understanding the mind an overall coherence which, again, he'd not recognized. In effect, his metapsychology. Metapsychology, a term coined by Freud, aims to bring together ‘“the fundamental concepts and principles” that underpin a theoretical model of the mind’ (p. 93). This is what Nettleton does with the works of Bollas.

In her Introduction, Nettleton writes that Bollas’ ‘picture of the mind was present, in essence, from the beginning of his writing. However, his overall model of the mind does not appear as a whole in any one place. The present book is an attempt to remedy this situation’ (p. 4). It is organized by themes and the 12 chapters are meant to be read consecutively.

ANALYST-PATIENT RELATIONSHIP, LACAN, MELANCHOLIA, TRANSFERENCE, THERAPEUTIC FRAME

According to French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan, psychosis is marked by a non-separation of the object a. Consequently, transference in psychosis remains at the level of duality and appears to have an inverted form, where it is the Other that looks for something in the patient and not vice versa. This makes the handling of transference challenging since there is no triangular structure that can mediate between the patient and the Other. The patient cannot rely on the Other to deal with difficult experiences of jouissance (marked by excess and senselessness). In this paper, we discuss our work with a patient following the logic of melancholic psychosis. Specifically, we discuss three types of interventions that aim to provide a space where the clinician can ‘manoeuvre’ within the transference, thus avoiding a relation that becomes persecutory or erotomaniacal in nature and providing the possibility of finding solutions in dealing with psychic suffering. First, we describe interventions aimed at incarnating a limited other. Second, interpreting the mad Other is discussed. Finally, we outline how the clinical work involves having an interest in the patient's affinities.

SUPERVISION, EXPERIENTIAL KNOWLEDGE, RESONANCE, INTERSUBJECTIVE SPACE, COMPETENCIES

Patients' personal experiences and the way in which they create an intersubjective space with significant others cannot be easily formulated and organized in semantic memories. Since the role of supervision is to reach and negotiate diverse types of knowledge, the author suggests, in this article, that for supervisors to acquire a deep understanding of patients' experiences, they need to become competent in helping their supervisees to identify, focus, and articulate their unique and valuable knowledge of the patients' unthought experiences. Supervisees' physical and mental presence in patients' struggle for recognition, influence and self-expression gives them access to types of knowledge that could not be reached in other ways. Supervisors, who have acquired this competency, are likely to create a more mutual and freer atmosphere, in the supervisory space, for considering and discussing various perspectives of patients' experiences. The author brings an example of how a supervisor and a supervisee sidestep the regular supervision discourse and articulate the supervisee's unformulated knowledge and of how they strive to integrate this knowledge with other existing knowledge about the patient and the therapeutic process.

HIKIKOMORI, ACUTE SOCIAL WITHDRAWAL, PSYCHIC RETREAT, PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, ADOLESCENCE

A hikikomori is a child, an adolescent or a young adult who voluntarily retreats into his own home for long periods, not showing evident signs of psychological distress or overt mental disorder. This phenomenon was first described in Japan, but several research studies show that it is spreading in many countries around the world. The author hypothesizes that the decision to become a hikikomori is made by the person in an attempt to find a solution to difficulties in relationships with himself and with others. The choice of reclusion rapidly becomes a trap: in this condition the individual is imprisoned in complex functions of the mind which curb and restrict independence and personal autonomy. This is owing to the fact that, with the withdrawal, a pathological personality organization, formed during the years of early infancy, gradually takes control of the internal world, pushing towards anti-developmental mental states and behaviours. The paper continues with some reflections on individual treatment with psychoanalytic psychotherapy of adolescents and young adults in a state of acute social withdrawal. The reference model used is John Steiner's notion of ‘psychic retreat’. A description of a four-year treatment completes the paper, allowing for further clinical reflections.

She has held a research scholarship at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and a research fellowship at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, Lausanne (EPFL). At EPFL, she wrote and taught a master's course on the nature of consciousness and its effects upon research methods. FAIRBAIRN, DUALISM, LIBIDO THEORY, PHILOSOPHY, PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY

In 1930 Fairbairn wrote ‘Libido theory re-evaluated’, which remained unpublished until 1994. It contains the beginnings of theoretical arguments that, I argue, resulted in his more famous 1940s papers. I posit that Fairbairn's 1930 critique of Freud's analytical dualist theoretical foundation is consistent with, and lays the ground for, his later work. Using the papers ‘Schizoid factors in the personality’ (1940), ‘The repression and return of bad objects’ (1943), ‘Endopsychic structure considered in terms of object-relationships’ (1944), and ‘Object-relationships and dynamic structure’ (1946), I show how Fairbairn's 1930 critique is relevant to his later propositions and elucidate Fairbairn's metatheoretical assumptions, about which he was not explicit after 1930. I argue that his theoretical propositions arise as a result of his longstanding, consistent critique that led him to replace analytical dualism with dynamical structure. Further, I argue that Klein, and Khan and Winnicott's criticism is unjustified; Fairbairn did not challenge the content of a theory he describes as ‘truths of fundamental importance’, he challenged its theorization. Because it resulted in his important theoretical propositions, Fairbairn's longstanding critique of libido theory is important within the history of psychoanalytic thought and deserves scholarly attention.

SYMBOLIC EQUATION, REPRESENTATION, PATHOLOGICAL PROJECTIVE IDENTIFICATIONS, NORMAL PROJECTIVE IDENTIFICATIONS, BOUNDARY CONFUSION, CONTAINING

Hanna Segal's original paper in 1957 on symbol-formation is a classic. It makes clinical observations of concrete symbolic equation and theorized the contrast with normal representation. In the process of developing the most accurate and most useful theory of symbol-formation that psychoanalysis possesses, Segal brought the psychoanalytic symbol into connection with the wider meaning of symbols in linguistics and other academic disciplines. It is less well known that she modified the theoretical conceptualization of her observations in the light of Bion's development of the theory of container-contained. Perhaps because of the clinical usefulness, little serious criticism has been made of either the original theory or its modification. In this paper, an appraisal will be made of these major conceptualizations. This paper looks again at the theory she used to make the distinction between normal symbols ‘proper’, or representations, and the concrete symbolic equation associated with the primitive or psychotic defences.

This paper is intended to offer a foundation for comparison of the approaches of Wilfred Bion and Donald Winnicott. SESSION FREQUENCY, TRAINING, PSYCHOANALYTIC IDENTITY, INTENSITY, RELATIONAL PSYCHOANALYSIS, INTERSUBJECTIVITY

Session frequency can be seen as definitive of psychoanalytic identity but contemporary relational and constructivist perspectives and trends towards psychoanalytic work being conducted at lower and varying frequencies are leading increasingly to a rift between psychoanalytic work as theorized and practised on the one hand and as ‘taught at’ specified frequencies within psychoanalytic institutions on the other. The value of high-frequency work in the right conditions is considered, while automatic equations between high-frequency, high-intensity and high-value clinical work are questioned. Pressure towards higher frequency work, sometimes to meet training requirements, may imperil the psychoanalytic stance it seeks to preserve, particularly the recognition of patients’ frequency preferences as a psychic phenomenon requiring understanding rather than manipulation. The roots of coercive attitudes to session frequency in unresolved issues relating to institutional psychoanalytic superegos are explored; implications for training, ethics and the status of psychoanalytic work are considered.

RESSENTIMENT, ENVY, TRANSVALUATION, GRIEVANCE, INJUSTICE

Using material from clinical practice and social research, this paper examines the many connections between the analysis of ressentiment provided by Nietzsche and Scheler and recent psychoanalytic analyses of grievance. Psychoanalysis has been particularly insightful regarding the process of ‘nursing’ grievance, something which illuminates both the righteousness of the anger involved and the yearning for an idealized past. It is argued that in their different ways both analyses explore blocked responses to perceived injustice and, whilst the emphasis in both cases is essentially upon how existential reality itself can be experienced as an injustice, Scheler's analysis also provides us with a way of understanding how ressentiment can be a response to real social injustices. Indeed social ressentiment is now widely regarded as the affective foundation of reactionary forms of populism.

Angela Foster  

Joanna Ryan has written a wide-ranging study of class and the failure of psychoanalysis to engage with this significant aspect of personal identity and lived experience. One might wonder if this is simply because when Freud was developing his theories he only lived and worked with people in similar social circumstances to himself, but this was not the case; he, like all of his contemporaries and the majority of his patients, had a nurse/nanny and other servants in both his family of origin and in his own household. Nor is it the case that he failed to see the differences or recognize the ways in which the relationship with one's nurse, who was often the primary carer, impacted on the psyche.

The author makes specific reference to Freud's emotional disturbance at the sudden disappearance of his own nurse and states: ‘The leap in Freud's text from these vivid memories and associations concerning his nurse to the bald, generalized statement of the Oedipus complex, without even a paragraph break, is indeed an aporia, into which the working class employee is propelled and thus abjected’ (p. 39). Ryan also provides an account of Freud's analysis of the Wolfman, who was compulsively attracted to working class women, and points out that Freud ‘suggests at this point that if all these servant girls were substitutes for the figure of his intellectually superior sister whom he had to forgo, then an intention to debase was contributing to his object choice’ (p. 43, emphasis in the original). This with the accompanying footnote that ‘Freud is pursuing an argument with Alfred Adler and his postulation of the primacy of power and prerogative … Adler, who worked contemporaneously and with a mainly working-class population of patients, described a symptomatic culture of inferiority complex, resulting from their socially underprivileged positions’ (p. 54).

Essentially, the author's argument is that Freud was engaged in disavowal and negation of both the women concerned and the importance of these early relationships in their own right. So we might be excused for concluding that Freud enacted rather than analysed these class differences. [See Coles (2015) for further analysis of the impact of nurse/nanny relationships on child development.] We know that if there is an aspect of our own experience that we cannot or will not examine, we are creating no-go areas for our patients. This, in my mind, is connected with the failure of psychoanalysis, until recently, to address social (as opposed to sexual) differences and especially differences in power (Foster, 2006).

COMPARATIVE METHOD, WORKING MODEL, THEORY OF CHANGE, IMPLICIT THEORY, CLINICAL COMMENTARY

There is now an extensive and highly developed literature within psychoanalysis on how best to understand the patients we work with, and their impact on the analyst or therapist, but far less on the mind of the clinician and how he or she thinks while working with the patient. One method for studying this, the Comparative Clinical Method developed by a group of European psychoanalysts, consists of a two-step model: after a careful description of the interventions made by the analyst, an attempt is made to construct what is taken to be the analyst's implicit working model, the internal template which he or she tacitly employs to conduct the analysis. In this paper I describe this model, which I then illustrate by taking a piece of published clinical material to show what an approach based on the Comparative Clinical Method might look like. Finally I make some comments on applying this model to the work of psychoanalytic psychotherapists.

This paper offers a brief résumé of Winnicott's approach to psychoanalysis through a reading that emphasizes his interest in the capacity to be as a fundamental acquisition of human subjectivity. This interest continued throughout his life. The paper argues that it is closely related to his interest in analytic communication and the emphasis in his paper ‘Communicating and not-communicating leading to a study of certain opposites’ of the importance clinically of the patient's right not to communicate and the analyst's acceptance of it. Three clinical vignettes are included to demonstrate Winnicott's way of working.

COUPLE THERAPY, NEUROSCIENCE, BLAME, PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, UNCONSCIOUS DYNAMICS, THERAPEUTIC CHANGE, MARITAL THERAPY, TRIANGULAR RELATIONSHIPS

This paper describes the process of couple therapy with two couples that used blame as the currency of exchange in their relationship. Both couples struggled with managing three-person relationships. The triangular setting of couple psychotherapy provoked and triggered primitive anxieties around exclusion, rejection and abandonment in both cases. I draw upon clinical work with two such couples to illustrate how one repeatedly collapsed the triangular space whereas the other gradually became more able to bear it. I refer to scientific evidence of the brain's ability to continue to change in response to new learning by forming fresh neural connections throughout life. I suggest that the repetitive occurrence of new experiences within couple psychotherapy can generate new neural pathways thereby biologically influencing new ways of how partners might respond to each other. I conclude by highlighting the therapeutic potential of the framework within which couple psychotherapy takes place, a triangular configuration which offers a developmental opportunity for navigating primitive anxieties related to triangular relationships.

Sian Ellis and Sue Hirst

Sue Hirst

AGIP
sian.ellis1@btinternet.com; hirstsuem@gmail.com

Sue Hirst  

Catherine Freeman, who died on 4 November 2017, was born in 1953 in a Normandy village near Mont St Michel. She came to London in the 1970s and was manager of Tuttons Brasserie, Covent Garden, in its early days. Then, in the 1980s, she trained as a psychiatric nurse and subsequently as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist.

In writing this Appreciation we have consulted with other colleagues and friends. From 1988 to 2008, Catherine worked as Staff Nurse and later Consultant Mental Health Nurse Specialist and Clinical Manager at the Halliwick Unit, an NHS psychotherapy service in Haringey, North London. Originally located at Friern Hospital, the Halliwick later moved to St Ann's Hospital in Tottenham, where it remains today as a well-respected service for people with personality disorder.

Anthony Bateman, who was appointed Consultant Psychiatrist and Consultant Psychotherapist at the Halliwick Unit in 1989, writes:

Catherine found that a psychotherapeutic approach to people with mental health problems fitted with her personal philosophy and her approach to the treatment of mental illness. She fitted Halliwick and Halliwick fitted her. In the late 1980s Halliwick unit lacked a clear identity in terms of who was being treated and how patients were treated. Catherine became central in re-directing the service as a specialist service for people with personality disorder and, over time, she was significant to the development of a cohesive team.

The team at Halliwick unit was organized along functional lines rather than professional lines. Catherine argued strongly to protect what she saw as the special skills of nurses who were also trained or were training in psychotherapy. She was concerned that managers and others in mental health services tended to diminish nurses and she was constantly sensitive to the potential for the profession to be undervalued. Indeed as a person she could be sensitive and sometimes reactive but she never lost a sense of proportion and her ability to laugh alongside herself was one of her great personal strengths.
